gloss: Desperate individuals willing to risk everything.
teaser: Today, we explore a phrase that captures the essence of risk and desperation.
script: Welcome to Chengyu Bites — your quick summary on Chinese 成语. Today, we explore a phrase that captures the essence of risk and desperation. [break 1s] The phrase is: 亡命之徒, wáng mìng zhī tú. [break 1s] 亡 (wáng) - to perish or to die, [break 0.5s] 命 (mìng) - life or fate, [break 0.5s] 之 (zhī) - of (a possessive particle), [break 0.5s] 徒 (tú) - person or individual. [break 1s] The full idiom is 亡命之徒, which literally means 'people who are risking their lives' and figuratively refers to desperate individuals willing to risk everything. [break 1s] Here’s the story behind it: [break 1.5s] In ancient China, there were tales of individuals who would go to extreme lengths to escape danger or pursue freedom. These people, often seen as outlaws, were considered to have nothing left to lose, hence their willingness to take great risks. Their stories became legends, leading to the term we use today, which reflects the idea of someone who has become desperate and reckless. [break 1.5s] Example one: 他是一个亡命之徒，常常违法。 [break 1s] He is a desperate individual who often breaks the law. [break 1s] Example two: 在这样的情况下，你必须变成亡命之徒。 [break 1s] In such a situation, you must become a desperate person. [break 1s] Example three: 他们是亡命之徒，为了自由而战。 [break 1s] They are desperate individuals fighting for freedom. [break 1s] So, remember: 亡命之徒 means desperate individuals willing to risk everything. Thank you for listening to Chengyu Bites! See you next time for another idiom. [break 1s]
